newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan says China diplomatic embargo irrational.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan says China diplomatic embargo irrational.

text.p: Taiwan said on Friday its senior officials were forced to conduct secret visits overseas because of rival China's "irrational" diplomatic embargo.
Pope John Paul has agreed to meet Taiwan's Vice President Lien Chan next Tuesday when Lien stops in Rome on his way back from a visit to Nicaragua, said Foreign Minister John Chang.
Lien will be the highest-ranking Taipei official to visit the Vatican, the island's only European ally, and meet the Pope.

Local media reported that Lien would extend his Central American mission to Europe, but officials were tight-lipped about Lien's itinerary after attending Friday's inauguration of Nicaraguan President Arnoldo Aleman.
Aside from the Vatican, state television said Lien would accept a honorary degree at a Belgian university.
"Mainland China has taken a very tough stance towards the Republic of China's activities in the international arena," Chang told reporters.
"Its attitude not only can be described as unreasonable, but also irrational. We are forced to take extra caution (in arranging high-level visits)," Chang added.
The Vatican, like Nicaragua, is one of only 30 states that recognise Taiwan's exiled Republic of China government instead of the rival communist Chinese government in Beijing.
Taiwan is worried that Beijing may pressure Italy not to issue transit visas to Lien and his entourage.
China has made representations to Washington for issuing a transit visa to Lien en route to Nicaragua and warned the United States not to create new damage to Sino-U.S. ties.

Senior Taiwanese officials have embarked on a series of damage-control visits overseas after South Africa, Taiwan's largest ally, announced last November it would sever ties with Taipei in favour of Beijing.
Taiwan and China have been arch rivals since a civil war split them in 1949. Beijing has tightened a diplomatic squeeze on Taipei in its quest to bring Taiwan under mainland rule.

Beijing has expressed a desire to improve ties with the Vatican, but says the Holy See first would have to sever links with Taiwan -- which Beijing regards as a renegade province ineligible for sovereign recognition.
China's officially atheist government refuses to allow the country's state-sanctioned Catholic church to swear allegiance to the Pope, insisting that it remain independent.
